title: The sealed room at Chidambaram
hookLine: a locked room at Chidambaram, palm leaves eaten by ants, and Tamil hymns that praise the Shiva of each town
carry: the tevaram: shiva praised in tamil, place by place
tomorrow: a wedding stopped by an old man with a deed.

lines: A KING WHO WANTS THE HYMNS.
ONLY THE SINGERS CAN OPEN IT.
cards: A sealed door in the great temple at Chidambaram, the temple of Shiva as the dancer. Behind it, tradition says, lies a room long left unopened. Outside stands a Chola king.
He has heard a few verses of the old Tamil hymns to Shiva sung at his court, and he wants the rest. The priests won't open the door.
Only the singers who made these hymns, they say, can open it, and those singers are long gone. A new part of the path begins here: the regional traditions, starting in the Tamil south.

teach.h: THE SAINTS CARRIED TO THE DOOR
teach.b: Here's the story, as tradition tells it, in paraphrase. If only the saints can open the door, the king will bring the saints.
He has images of the three singers, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, carried through the streets in procession and set before the room. The door opens.
Inside are the palm leaves the hymns were written on, much of them eaten away by white ants.

teach.h: WHAT THIS AGE NEEDS WAS KEPT
teach.b: Then, the story says, a voice is heard: what this age needs has been kept. A learned devotee, Nambi Andar Nambi, gathers what survives and sets it in order, and the hymns are sung again.
That gathering is the Tevaram, at the heart of the Tirumurai, the Tamil Shaiva canon. The story doesn't pretend nothing was lost; the ants got there first. And look at the hymns themselves.
They're in Tamil, not Sanskrit, and they're tied to places.

teach.h: THE SHIVA OF THIS PLACE, IN TAMIL
teach.b: A hymn praises the Shiva of this town, by this river, in this grove. The singers walked from shrine to shrine, and the temples they sang are still known as the places that were sung. Here's the teaching.
Hindus believe the one God, present everywhere, also truly dwells in a particular temple, in a particular form, and can be praised in your own mother tongue.
That's why temple singers, oduvars, still sing these Tamil hymns in worship. And in the story, the key to the room was the singers themselves.

how: In Tamil Shaiva temples, singers called oduvars sing hymns from the Tevaram during worship.

games.q: what does “tamil shaivism and the tevaram” mean?
o: a Tamil festival of lamps lit for Shiva each winter
the Tamil hymns to Shiva at the heart of Tamil Shaivism
a Sanskrit law book followed in Tamil Shiva temples

games.q: your family visits a temple in India your grandparents loved. a cousin says God is everywhere, so why travel? by the Tevaram, what fits?
o: God is everywhere, and also truly met in this place; the hymns praise the Lord of each town.
God lives only in temples, nowhere else.
the trip is just sightseeing; the place doesn't matter.
games.why: the Tevaram sings the Shiva of this town, this river, this tank. everywhere, and here.

practice: Bring to mind one temple, shrine or home altar you know: its smell, its light, the sound of it. Greet God there the way the Tevaram does, as the Lord of that place, the one who lives right there.
If you know a line of a hymn in your family's language, say it softly. If you don't pray, picture the place and what it holds for the people who go there, and give thanks for what was kept.

wordCard.voice: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: the hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, sung place by place and, tradition says, rescued from a sealed room at Chidambaram. Today's word.

orig.note: Tamil. the Tevaram, the hymns of the three Tamil Shaiva singers.
